tldr: We present POIL, a framework that transfers skills from a single demonstration to novel objects and reliably converges to the goal under external disturbances using closed-loop control with stable dynamical systems.
hero_caption: Overview of POIL. In the transfer stage (left), a multi-modal LLM grounds functional parts, and demonstrated point trajectories are geometrically mapped to the target object. In the execution stage (right), Point-set BCSDM operates on online-tracked point sets, solving for a single rigid-body twist to drive the robot in closed loop.
overview:
When robots perform new tasks in unseen environments, one-shot imitation learning offers an appealing way to avoid collecting extensive demonstration datasets. However, achieving success in the real world poses two major hurdles: transferring a single demonstration across novel shapes and object categories, and executing it robustly in closed loop despite grasp pose variations or external disturbances. Existing trajectory transfer methods often rely on open-loop replay. Conversely, stable dynamical systems that handle disturbances typically require known 3D CAD models or accurate 6D pose estimators ahead of time.

To tackle both challenges, this work introduces POIL (Point-based One-Shot Imitation Learning), which uses a shared representation: 3D point sets on the object's functional parts (regions involved in the task). In the transfer stage, a multi-modal LLM grounds parts like "mug handle" via text queries, establishing point correspondences to novel objects such as teapots or bags and generating object-centric trajectories free from gripper pose constraints. During execution, Point-set BCSDM—an extension of stable dynamical models from SE(3) poses to point sets—acts on online-tracked points from cameras. By projecting per-point velocity vectors onto a single rigid-body twist (linear and angular velocity), it achieves closed-loop control with almost-global asymptotic stability (mathematical convergence guarantees) toward the goal, without needing a full 3D model of the object.

In simulation and real-robot experiments on a Franka Panda arm, POIL demonstrated high task success rates across cross-category transfers (from mugs to bags or trays), unseen grasp poses, modified rack geometries, and active human physical disturbances during execution.
contributions: Leveraging a 3D point set on the functional part as a shared representation to simultaneously achieve flexible one-shot object generalization and closed-loop convergence guarantees.

Developing Point-set BCSDM by extending existing SE(3) pose-based stable dynamical systems to point clouds, and theoretically proving that its terminal phase acts as a gradient flow on an SO(3) potential with almost-global asymptotic stability under a rigid-object assumption.

Bypassing dense feature matching that fails under severe viewpoint changes and self-occlusions, in favor of a text-driven functional part grounding pipeline combining a multi-modal LLM with multi-view prompting.

sections.heading: Why Does One-Shot Trajectory Transfer Need Stable Dynamical Systems?
sections.summary: In one-shot imitation learning aimed at novel object generalization, unifying trajectory transfer with closed-loop convergence guarantees has remained unexplored. POIL bridges this gap using 3D point sets on object functional parts as a shared representation.
sections.details:
One-shot imitation learning in robot manipulation largely falls into two camps: adapting pre-trained policies, or directly transferring demonstrated trajectories to new scenes via semantic correspondences. The former requires expensive action-labeled data and struggles with out-of-distribution generalization. Trajectory transfer is thus an attractive alternative for leaping to novel shapes and categories.

However, most prior trajectory transfer works simply solve static correspondences between demonstration and target scenes, followed by open-loop replay. This breaks down whenever the target object shifts, a different grasp pose must be used, or external disturbances occur during execution. Even if feedback control is added to correct offsets, there is no guarantee that the system will converge to the goal when knocked far off course.

This is where stable dynamical systems excel. They construct autonomous vector fields that guide states toward target points, guaranteeing convergence from arbitrary initial states. Yet, traditional stable dynamical systems rely on known 3D CAD models or runtime pose estimators, separating them from one-shot transfer to novel objects. POIL bridges these two capabilities by grounding both transfer and execution in a single representation: 3D point sets placed on an object's functional parts.

captions.F1: System overview of POIL. In the offline transfer stage (left), functional parts are identified via language grounding to generate point trajectories. In the online execution stage (right), Point-set BCSDM computes stable rigid-body twists in real time from tracked point clouds.

sections.heading: At the Intersection of One-Shot Imitation, Keypoint Representations, and Stable Dynamical Systems
sections.summary: We review three related research threads: one-shot imitation, keypoint representations, and stable dynamical systems. POIL brings them together to achieve pre-training-free novel object generalization alongside model-free closed-loop convergence guarantees.
sections.details:
### II-A One-Shot Imitation Learning
Existing one-shot imitation methods either adapt policies pre-trained on action-labeled data or transfer trajectories geometrically and semantically without policy training. The former is bounded by training data coverage. The latter enables cross-category transfer, but most works rely on open-loop execution; closed-loop variants have largely focused on in-category initial pose alignment.

### II-B Keypoint Representations for Manipulation
Keypoints are widely used to summarize state in a compact, object-centric way. However, conventional approaches often require task-specific detector pre-training. Foundation-model approaches (like ReKep and MOKA) solve geometric constraints without demonstrations, differing from direct demonstration transfer. Methods like RoboTAP and Point Policy track points for closed-loop control, but they lack formal convergence guarantees.

### II-C Stable Dynamical Systems
Stable dynamical systems design time-invariant autonomous velocity fields that ensure goal convergence under disturbances. In robot manipulation, these systems have historically treated a single SE(3) pose of an object or gripper as state, demanding known 3D CAD models or accurate pose estimators. BCSDM, the foundation of this work, reconciles behavior controllability and stability on SE(3), but still drives gripper poses directly. POIL extends this formulation to point sets of novel objects, enabling model-free stable control.

sections.heading: Inside POIL: From Language-Grounded Parts to Point-Set BCSDM Control
sections.summary: In the transfer stage, a multi-modal LLM with multi-view prompting extracts functional parts and adapts point trajectories to target objects and new fixtures. In the execution stage, Point-set BCSDM solves for rigid-body twists from point-wise velocity fields for stable control.
sections.details:
POIL extracts 3D points on functional parts from multi-view RGB-D demonstration videos, maps them to the target object, and drives them with a stable dynamical system during tracking.

### III-A Point Trajectory Transfer
The pipeline begins with functional part grounding. Dense visual feature matching often fails under large viewpoint or shape variations. Instead, POIL uses the open-vocabulary detector Rex-Omni to identify parts using semantic text queries (e.g., "mug handle"). To prevent misdetections from self-occlusion in individual views, a "multi-view prompt" bundles images from multiple viewpoints into a single grid. The resulting bounding boxes are segmented with SAM2 and projected to 3D point clouds using depth maps.

From the demonstration point set $\mathcal{P}_{\text{demo}}$, $N_k=10$ points are sampled via farthest point sampling. A combination of coarse rigid-plus-anisotropic scale transformation and occlusion-aware non-rigid registration (OAReg) maps these points to the target point set $\mathcal{P}_{\text{tgt}}$. The demonstration point trajectories, recorded by a robust RGB-D point tracker (MVTracker), are transferred to the target points. When destination fixtures (racks) differ in shape, a few user-clicked correspondences allow Thin Plate Spline (TPS) warping to smoothly adapt the trajectory to the new geometry.

### III-B Closed-Loop Execution via Point-set BCSDM
At runtime, the robot does not need to reproduce the demonstration grasp. Because control is defined relative to the functional part, any feasible grasp avoiding collisions and joint limits can be used. Part symmetry (e.g., 180-degree ambiguity) is resolved geometrically to select the optimal correspondence.

During online control, BCSDM generates a velocity vector for each tracked point $x_i$. The trade-off between nominal trajectory tracking and goal convergence is adjusted by parameter $\eta$ (set to $\eta=3$ in experiments). Under the assumption of a rigid grasp, the per-point velocities $\{v_i\}$ are projected onto a single rigid-body twist $(v, \omega)$ around the center of mass using least squares with RANSAC for outlier rejection.

### Theoretical Stability Proof
Under the rigid-object assumption, the authors analyze the stability of rotational motion in the terminal phase. Projecting per-point velocity errors into a rigid rotational velocity via least squares is mathematically identical to gradient descent on the classical SO(3) navigation function $D(R) = \operatorname{tr}(W(I-R))$, where $W$ is the inertia-like matrix computed from the tracked points. Aside from the goal orientation $R=I$, this potential has three critical points, all of which are unstable saddle points rather than local minima. As a result, almost-global asymptotic stability is guaranteed, converging to the target orientation from all initial states except for a set of measure zero.

captions.F3: Trajectory adaptation under modified environment fixtures (racks). Given a few clicked correspondences between the straight demonstration rack (left) and the target L-shaped rack (right), the TPS deformation field $\Phi$ smoothly warps the entire trajectory to the new geometry.

sections.heading: Simulation and Real-Robot Validation: Novel Objects, Disturbances, and Geometry Changes
sections.summary: After evaluating part transfer accuracy and controller robustness individually, the complete pipeline was validated in simulation and on a Franka Panda robot. It maintained a 100% success rate across unseen initial poses and successfully transferred mug demonstrations to bags and trays with disturbance recovery.
sections.details:
Evaluation was carried out across three stages: point transfer accuracy, controller robustness, and end-to-end pipeline validation.

### IV-A Functional Part Point Transfer Accuracy
POIL was compared against dense feature matching using DINOv2 and DIFT. As viewpoint offsets grew from 30 to 90 degrees, feature-based methods suffered sharp increases in error, whereas POIL's text-grounded approach maintained the lowest point error across all angles. An ablation replacing the multi-view prompt with single-view processing verified its effectiveness in suppressing false detections.

### IV-B Pose Robustness with Point-set BCSDM
Across four tasks with varying geometric complexity (PnP Cube, Book Insertion, Mug Hanging, and Bag Hanging), the controller was evaluated against Point Policy (a point-based BC baseline) and Instant Policy (a motion prior model). Starting from initial poses near the demonstration distribution ("Near") and far from it ("Far"), Point Policy failed out-of-distribution even when trained on 50 demos, while Instant Policy struggled on complex insertion tasks. In contrast, Point-set BCSDM achieved a 100% success rate across all tasks and distances using only a single demonstration.

### IV-C End-to-End Evaluation and Real-Robot Experiments
In simulation, POIL demonstrated disturbance recovery during teapot pouring and accommodated different grasp poses when inserting a toppled mug onto a rack. Across 50 random pose trials, 39 succeeded; failures stemmed from part detection misses (7 runs) or lack of feasible IK grasps (3 runs), confirming that the point-set controller itself remained stable. Trajectory adaptation to tall boxes and L-shaped racks was also validated.

On the real Franka Panda arm, a simulated mug-hanging demonstration was transferred to a real mug, a brown handbag, and a green paper bag. Because the handbag had elongated straps, its points were matched with a roughly 90-degree in-plane rotation; however, in-plane rotational freedom allowed it to hang successfully. Furthermore, a human demonstration of placing a tray on a rack was transferred to wooden trays and bags. In sim-to-real mug hanging, POIL achieved 6 out of 10 successes (3 tracking losses, 1 IK failure). When a human experimenter forcibly rotated the cup mid-motion, the online point tracker immediately recovered and guided the object back on track.

Bottom: Transfer from a human demonstration of tray placement to a wooden tray and a bag, executing motions along tracked point trajectories (blue-to-red gradient).

sections.heading: Conclusions and Limitations: Diversifying Grasps and Pushing Tracking Boundaries
sections.summary: POIL unifies one-shot trajectory transfer with stable closed-loop control via functional part point sets, achieving model-free almost-global convergence. Remaining challenges include maintaining tracking through severe occlusions and expanding beyond single-grasp planning.
sections.details:
POIL addresses both the fragility of open-loop trajectory replay and the reliance of stable dynamical systems on known 3D models or pose estimators by adopting 3D point sets on functional parts as a unified representation. Experiments in simulation and on real hardware demonstrate robustness across object categories, grasp variations, environmental geometry changes, and physical external disturbances.

The authors also outline several assumptions and limitations:
- The pipeline requires text queries for part detection and a few manual point clicks when destination fixtures change significantly.
- Online point tracking can fail if objects leave camera view, suffer severe occlusions, or feature transparent/specular surfaces causing depth dropouts.
- The system assumes a single static grasp with a parallel-jaw gripper, which may fail to find collision-free, IK-feasible solutions when an object is placed in extreme orientations.

Future work includes incorporating regrasp behaviors across multi-stage execution and extending the framework to multi-fingered hand manipulation.

takeaways: Anchoring control to an object's functional parts (such as handles) rather than end-effector poses provides grasp flexibility and enables seamless transfer across novel objects and categories.

Projecting per-point velocity fields onto a single rigid-body twist via least squares aligns mathematically with gradient flow on a classical SO(3) navigation function, providing almost-global asymptotic stability without 3D CAD models.
Under large viewpoint variations and rotations, language-grounded part detection paired with multi-view prompts proves far more reliable than dense visual feature matching like DINOv2.
limitations: The system relies on online point tracking (MVTracker), which fails under blind spots, severe self-occlusions, or depth sensor noise from transparent and reflective surfaces.
Assuming a single static parallel-jaw grasp can lead to execution failures if extreme object poses leave no collision-free, IK-feasible grasp.
Significant changes in destination geometry (such as custom racks or hooks) still require a few manual point correspondences.
